title: Redwood throughput tuning - technical deep dive
summary: Deep dive on throughput tuning for BrightScale production workload: continuous batching, scheduler knobs, max_num_seqs, token limits, KV cache behavior, quantization tradeoffs and VPC/on-prem considerations. Agreed next steps include benchmark runs with specified knobs, sharing perf spreadsheet and security docs.
action_items: Marcus - run 3x 1hr perf runs with max_num_seqs=32,64,128 and token_limit=1024 by 2026-09-21
Lena - send perf spreadsheet and pricing bands for dedicated capacity by 2026-09-16
Ravi - provide current traffic distribution and p95 latency SLOs by 2026-09-18

Marcus to attach yamls used for scheduler knobs in Slack
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-14
Time: 14:30 PT
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Lena (Redwood AE), Marcus (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood SRE), Tom (BrightScale CTO), Eve (BrightScale ML), Ravi (BrightScale Infra), Maya (BrightScale PM)

[00:00] Lena: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um, we'll jump straight in. The goal today is to walk through throughput tuning levers — continuous batching, scheduler knobs, max_num_seqs, token limits — and show how those interact with KV cache and quantization choices.

[00:22] Tom: sounds good, we're mainly trying to get predictable throughput for our chat and summarization pipelines, p95 latency target is 300ms but we're okay if p95 bumps to ~600ms during spikes as long as cost doesn't blow up.

[00:38] Marcus: cool, can you quick remind us of your current traffic profile? average qps, seq lengths?

[00:44] Eve: sure, right now at peak we see ~120 qps, typical sequence lengths 40-100 tokens for chat, summarization runs average 320 tokens. We do a mix of short and long. Most requests are single-turn chat but some are multi-turn with KV cache enabled on our current in-house runner.

[01:05] Priya: and you said p95 300ms, is that for hosted endpoints or your on-prem infra?

[01:10] Tom: this is for whatever we move to — ideally hosted Redwood first, then maybe private. We need to evaluate dedicated vs hosted for cost predictability.

[01:18] Marcus: ok makes sense. quick note on terms — when I say continuous batching I'm referring to the server-side scheduler that's allowed to hold a request for a short time window to batch more tokens, sometimes called the "latency budget" knob in our console. The main knobs to tune are max_num_seqs (max sequences per batch), token_limit (max tokens per batch), and the batching window in ms.

[01:42] Eve: we've been conservative with batching, set max_seq to 8 on our self-host which reduced p50 but killed throughput.

[01:49] Marcus: yep that tracks. There's always a tradeoff: smaller max_num_seqs reduces tail latency but increases per-token cost because you get smaller batches. For your traffic mix with many short sequences, increasing continuous batching window slightly helps.

[02:05] Tom: can you give ballpark numbers — if we go from max_num_seqs 8 to 64 what happens?

[02:11] Marcus: rough rule: throughput scales sub-linearly with batch size because of kernel/attention overheads and KV cache locality. For example in our benchmarks on A100s, going 8 -> 32 gave ~2.1x throughput with p95 increasing maybe 1.6x; 32 -> 64 gave another 1.4x. But the exact numbers depend on sequence lengths and quantization.

[02:35] Lena: also worth flagging the KV cache behavior — if you have many multi-turns that hit the same KV keys we see better effective throughput because the runtime can reuse KV and avoid recompute. But if sequences are cold, larger batches won't save the KV warmup cost.

[02:52] Eve: we do a lot of multi-turn for chat, so KV reuse should help, but our user base has many unique sessions so cache hit isn't perfect.

[03:03] Marcus: I'd recommend running a perf test with two traffic shapes: mix A (50% short chat 40 tokens, 50% long summary 320 tokens) and mix B (heavy multi-turn with persistent sessions). That tells us how contention and KV caching affect effective throughput.

[03:20] Tom: what about token_limit? we saw one of your docs mention token_limit per batch — how do we set that?

[03:27] Marcus: token_limit caps total tokens in the batch. If you set token_limit low you prevent huge batches from forming when there's a long tail of long requests. For your mix, setting token_limit around 1024-2048 keeps long summaries from dominating. For continuous batching window, small windows (10-25ms) help maintain low p95 while still improving batching for short requests.

[03:49] Priya: are there scheduler knobs exposed in the private deployment too? we prefer same knobs across hosted and private.

[03:55] Marcus: yes, the scheduler parameters are consistent. In private you control them via the runtime config yaml. In hosted they're in the Console under "Serving -> Scheduler". We also have an auto-tuner that suggests values based on historical traces.

[04:12] Eve: quick question on quantization — we quantized to int8 on our runner and lost some quality on summarization. How aggressive can we go?

[04:20] Marcus: quantization tradeoffs are model-specific. For many of the open models we certify a few quantization profiles: fp16, int8, q4_0, q4_1, etc. In our tests q4_0 often gives ~2x speedup with small quality delta for classification and chat, but summarization can be sensitive — we recommend running your eval prompts against each quant profile. We'll share the quantization compatibility matrix.

[04:45] Tom: do quantized runs affect KV cache behavior?

[04:48] Marcus: not really at the logical level — the KV cache is bytes of hidden states; quantization affects execution kernels but the cache still stores and keys by sequence. However the memory footprint changes and that can change how many sequences you can store in cache before evictions. So quantization can indirectly help KV capacity.

[05:06] Maya: and for on-prem, what about GPU choices? we have H100s and some older A40 nodes. any guidance?

[05:13] Marcus: H100s give best throughput and smaller kernel latency for long sequences; A40/A100 are fine for mixed loads. The runtime will pick kernels optimized for the device. If you plan on on-prem, pooling similar GPUs and giving the scheduler aware of hardware type helps. We also advise pinning model variants to device classes in the deployment config.

[05:33] Ravi: about VPC/private networking — we need to preserve data residency and use our KMS. Does Redwood Private integrate with HSM/KMS?

[05:41] Lena: yes, Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS and HSM via standard integrations, and audit logs are available. We'll include the security docs.

[05:49] Eve: can we get a rough cost/throughput estimate for hosted vs dedicated?

[05:53] Lena: we'll send pricing bands. For throughput tuning specifically, dedicated reserved pools give best unit economics at scale because you avoid per-token hosted overheads and can tune batching aggressively. Hosted is better to start with for quick tests.

[06:08] Marcus: one more note — the scheduler has a backpressure knob: max_inflight_per_worker. If you tune that down you avoid queuing bursts that blow p95, but you reduce peak throughput. For BrightScale's profile with mix of short/long, I suggest starting with max_num_seqs=64, token_limit=2048, batching_window=20ms, and max_inflight_per_worker=8 for dedicated pools. Then adjust based on observed p95 and cost.

[06:35] Tom: ok that sounds actionable. can you summarize recommended test matrix?

[06:38] Marcus: sure — run three experiments: (A) conservative low-latency: max_num_seqs=8, window=5-10ms, token_limit=1024; (B) balanced: max_num_seqs=32, window=15-25ms, token_limit=2048; (C) throughput-first: max_num_seqs=64-128, window=30-50ms, token_limit=4096. For each run collect p50/p95/p99, tokens/sec, cost estimate and KV hit ratio. Also run each under two quant profiles (fp16 and q4_0).

[07:12] Eve: helpful. Marcus, can you run the first set or provide the YAML?

[07:16] Marcus: yes I'll put the exact runtime yaml in Slack and run a couple quick smoke tests. Then we'll hand over the scripts for you to run in your environment.

[07:24] Lena: ok next steps: Marcus will run the baseline and share yamls; I'll share perf spreadsheet and pricing; Ravi will send traffic distribution; schedule follow-up wk of 9/28.

[07:35] Tom: great, thanks everyone.

[07:38] Maya: thanks, bye.
